section.title: Laws Concerning Vows
section.sectionRationale: Coming right after the festival calendar, this short law addresses a very personal question: what happens when someone makes a vow to the LORD. It matters enough to God that He gives careful, specific instruction protecting the seriousness of a spoken vow while also defining real, limited exceptions within a household.
section.thesis: A man's vow to the LORD must never be broken, and while a woman still under her father's or husband's authority may have her vow confirmed or nullified by him on the day he hears it, once that window passes, or once a vow stands unchallenged, it holds with the same binding weight as any other vow before God.
section.frameNote: Two movements: the unconditional binding force of a man's vow; and the specific, time-limited role a father or husband plays in confirming or nullifying the vow of a daughter or wife still under his household authority.

units.label: A vow must not be broken
units.note: he must do everything he has promised

verses.text: Then Moses said to the heads of the tribes of Israel, “This is what the LORD has commanded:
If a man makes a {{vow|vow}} to the LORD or swears an oath to obligate himself by a pledge, he must not break his word; he must do everything he has promised.

media.alt: A father and daughter standing quietly at a doorway on a still evening
media.caption: A vow made under a father's roof, confirmed by his silence.

verses.text: And if a woman in her father's house during her youth makes a vow to the LORD or obligates herself by a pledge,
and her father hears about her vow or pledge but says nothing to her, then all the vows or pledges by which she has bound herself shall stand.

But if her father prohibits her on the day he hears about it, then none of the vows or pledges by which she has bound herself shall stand. The LORD will absolve her because her father has prohibited her.

units.label: A wife's vow
units.note: her husband may confirm or {{nullify|nullify}} it

verses.text: If a woman marries while under a vow or rash promise by which she has bound herself,
and her husband hears of it but says nothing to her on that day, then the vows or pledges by which she has bound herself shall stand.
But if her husband prohibits her when he hears of it, he nullifies the vow that binds her or the rash promise she has made, and the LORD will absolve her.
Every vow a widow or divorced woman pledges to fulfill is binding on her.
If a woman in her husband's house has made a vow or put herself under an obligation with an oath,
and her husband hears of it but says nothing to her and does not prohibit her, then all the vows or pledges by which she has bound herself shall stand.

But if her husband nullifies them on the day he hears of them, then nothing that came from her lips, whether her vows or pledges, shall stand. Her husband has nullified them, and the LORD will absolve her.
Her husband may confirm or nullify any vow or any sworn pledge to deny herself.
But if her husband says nothing to her from day to day, then he confirms all the vows and pledges that bind her. He has confirmed them, because he said nothing to her on the day he heard about them.
But if he nullifies them after he hears of them, then he will bear her iniquity.”
These are the statutes that the LORD commanded Moses concerning the relationship between a man and his wife, and between a father and a young daughter still in his home.

vow.gloss: A vow, a voluntary promise made to God. A neder was never required, but once spoken, Scripture treats it with utmost seriousness, since it invokes God's own name and character as witness to the pledge, Deuteronomy 23:21-23.

nullify.gloss: To break, annul, or nullify. This law grants a father or husband a narrow, time-bound power to parar, nullify, a dependent woman's vow on the very day he learns of it, after which the window closes and the vow, if unchallenged, holds with full force.

basic.context: This short chapter gives Israel a specific law about vows, voluntary promises made to God. A man's vow always binds him completely. A woman still living under her father's or husband's authority has a narrow window in which he may nullify her vow, but if he says nothing on the day he hears it, or if any window passes, the vow stands exactly as binding as any other.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a real legal statute regulating vows within Israel's specific household and covenant structure. It reflects the household authority patterns of its ancient context while still taking women's own spoken vows with real seriousness, since even a nullified vow required the LORD's own absolution, not merely a father's or husband's dismissal.
basic.originalLanguages: A neder, vow, once spoken to the LORD, carries binding weight because it calls on God's own name and character. The specific power given to a father or husband to parar, nullify, is narrow and time-limited, valid only on the very day he hears of it, after which his silence itself confirms the vow with full force.
basic.typology: The seriousness with which God treats every spoken word offered to Him anticipates Jesus' own teaching that a simple yes or no should be as binding as any oath, Matthew 5:33-37, since the character of the speaker, not elaborate vow-making, is what should guarantee truthful, faithful speech.
basic.christ: While this chapter contains no direct messianic prophecy, its insistence that a spoken vow to God must be honored completely reflects the same unwavering faithfulness to His own word that God shows throughout Scripture, ultimately embodied in Christ, who is Himself described as the amen, the faithful and true witness, in whom every promise of God is guaranteed, Revelation 3:14, 2 Corinthians 1:20.
basic.god: God takes human speech directed to Him with total seriousness, holding people to their word even when it costs them, while also building in real, limited protections for those under another's household authority. His concern for the vulnerable and His insistence on integrity of speech operate together in the same law.
basic.crossReferences: Deuteronomy 23:21-23 reinforces that a vow, though never required, must be kept once made. Ecclesiastes 5:4-5 warns that it is better not to vow than to vow and not fulfill it. Matthew 5:33-37 has Jesus teach that truthful, simple speech should make elaborate vows unnecessary altogether.
basic.oneStory: God cares deeply about the integrity of every word spoken to Him, holding people to their vows while making real, careful provision for those under another's authority. This concern for truthful speech runs through Scripture to Jesus, whose own faithful word never fails, and in whom every promise of God finds its unshakeable yes.

context.literary:
The chapter is a tightly built piece of case law. Verse 1 introduces it, verse 2 states the governing principle for a man, verses 3 to 15 work through four cases for women, and verse 16 closes with a summary. The four cases are a young woman in her father's house, verses 3 to 5; a woman who marries while a vow is still on her, verses 6 to 8; a widow or divorced woman, verse 9; and a wife who vows while in her husband's house, verses 10 to 15.

Each case follows the same two branch pattern. If the father or husband 'hears' and 'says nothing,' the vows 'shall stand.' If he 'prohibits' or 'nullifies' on the day he hears, they do not stand and 'the LORD will absolve her.' The verbs hear, say nothing, stand, prohibit and absolve repeat until the listener could recite them. The phrase 'on the day he hears' recurs in verses 5, 7, 12 and 14, making time the hinge of the whole law.

The short widow's case of verse 9 sits almost at the centre and throws light on the rest. A woman with no father or husband over her is bound exactly as a man is in verse 2. The final paragraph then adds a twist in verse 15: a husband who cancels a vow late 'will bear her iniquity.'

The chapter is linked to what comes before by the mention of 'vow and freewill offerings' in Numbers 29:39, and it is unusual in being addressed to 'the heads of the tribes,' verse 1, the men responsible for households and clans. It also foreshadows chapter 31, where Israel's army returns from Midian and brings an offering of gold to the LORD, Numbers 31:50.
context.historical:
Vows were a normal part of Israelite piety. A person in need would promise God a gift or an act of devotion if He answered, as Jacob did at Bethel, Genesis 28:20-22, or Hannah at Shiloh, 1 Samuel 1:11. Leviticus 27 sets out how vowed persons, animals, houses and fields could be valued and redeemed, and Numbers 6 describes the special vow of the Nazirite, open to 'a man or woman,' Numbers 6:2.

A vow usually had a cost. It might mean an animal from the flock, money from the household, time away at the sanctuary, or a period of fasting, which is what verse 13 has in view with a pledge 'to deny herself,' literally to afflict her soul. In a household economy where the father or husband carried legal responsibility for property and for the family's obligations, a wife's or daughter's vow could commit resources that were not hers alone. The law gives the head of the house one day to respond, so that no one is left in suspense and no household is bound by a promise its head has not heard.

Israel's story shows why this mattered. Jephthah's vow in Judges 11:30-31 ended in grief, 'I have given my word to the LORD and cannot take it back,' Judges 11:35. Saul's rash oath in 1 Samuel 14:24 nearly cost Jonathan his life. Hannah's vow, by contrast, is kept with her husband's consent: Elkanah answers, 'may the LORD confirm His word,' 1 Samuel 1:23, using the same verb 'confirm' that Numbers 30:14 uses of a husband who lets a vow stand.

By the time of Jesus, vows had become an instrument of evasion. Mark 7:11-12 describes a son declaring his support 'Corban,' devoted to God, so that he no longer had to help his parents.
context.canonical:
The chapter stands in a line of Scripture on vows. Leviticus 5:4 already treated a thoughtless oath as a matter needing atonement. Deuteronomy 23:21-23 adds the key balance: vowing is voluntary, 'if you refrain from making a vow, you will not be guilty of sin,' but a vow made must be kept, 'what comes from your lips.' Ecclesiastes 5:4-6 repeats the warning and tells the worshipper not to tell the messenger 'that your vow was a mistake.'

The Psalms show vows as part of glad worship. 'I will fulfill my vows to the LORD in the presence of all His people,' Psalm 116:14. The righteous person of Psalm 15:4 'does not revise a costly oath.' Psalm 22:25, the psalm that begins with the cry Jesus spoke on the cross, ends in the great assembly: 'I will fulfill my vows before those who fear You.' Jonah in the fish promises, 'I will fulfill what I have vowed,' Jonah 2:9. Proverbs 20:25 warns that it is 'a trap for a man to dedicate something rashly.'

In the New Testament the BSB footnote notes that Numbers 30:2 is cited in Matthew 5:33, where Jesus sums up the old teaching, 'Do not break your oath, but fulfill your vows to the Lord,' and then presses behind it: 'let your Yes be Yes,' Matthew 5:37. James 5:12 echoes Him. Jesus also exposes the scribal system of oaths that distinguished binding from non binding formulas, Matthew 23:16-22. Yet the practice of vows did not disappear at once; Paul kept a vow at Cenchrea, Acts 18:18, and joined men under a vow in Jerusalem, Acts 21:23-24.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses wanted Israel to grasp that speech addressed to God is not casual. A vow is a word 'that came from her lips,' verse 12, or 'everything he has promised,' literally all that goes out of his mouth, verse 2. God hears it, and God holds the speaker to it. Israel was about to enter a land where the temptation would be to make pious promises in a crisis and forget them in prosperity. This law closed that door.

At the same time Moses wanted the heads of households to handle their authority with speed and honesty. The father or husband is not given unlimited power. He must act 'on the day he hears,' or his silence becomes consent. If he tries to cancel a vow later, the guilt falls on him, not on her, verse 15. The point is not that women's words matter less, but that household obligations must be settled openly and at once.

The law also showed God's kindness. A young woman who spoke beyond her means, or a new wife bound by a promise made before marriage, was not left trapped. When her vow was lawfully set aside, 'the LORD will absolve her,' verses 5, 8 and 12. God Himself releases her. The first hearers were to learn that God is both strict about truth and merciful in the way He applies it.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter is prescriptive law for Israel, framed by the household structure of that time, in which a father or husband carried legal responsibility for the family's property and obligations. Christians are not bound to its procedure, and the church does not have a sanctuary where vowed animals are offered. Nor does the chapter command that a husband today should review his wife's promises to God.

What carries over is the principle, which Jesus deepens rather than cancels. Every word spoken before God matters, Matthew 5:37, and wedding vows, ordination vows, membership vows and baptismal promises still carry real weight. Those with responsibility for others must use it quickly, openly and fairly, and bear the cost if they abuse it, as verse 15 teaches. Believers should be slow to make promises, Ecclesiastes 5:2, and faithful in keeping them even at cost, Psalm 15:4. And where a promise was rash or sinful, the gospel answer is not to pretend it never happened, but to bring it to God, who is able to absolve.

debates.question: Does this law treat women's words before God as worth less than men's?

views.label: The law protects women and takes their vows seriously
views.case: A woman's vow is binding in itself; the widow and divorced woman of verse 9 are held to their word exactly as a man is in verse 2. The father's or husband's role is limited to one day, and if he cancels late he 'will bear her iniquity,' verse 15. When a vow is lawfully set aside, God Himself absolves her. On this reading the law protects a dependent woman from being trapped by an obligation she could not fulfil without her household's resources.

views.label: The law reflects the patriarchal structure of its time
views.case: Others emphasise that the difference in treatment rests on the social and economic order of ancient Israel, where women generally lived under a father or husband and did not hold property independently. On this view the law is a humane regulation within that order rather than a timeless statement about how men and women relate before God, and it should not be used as a pattern for control in marriage today.

debates.bearing: The two views overlap more than they disagree. Both see that the law assumes an ancient household economy, and both see that it takes a woman's vow as a real act before God, limits the authority of the man and guards her from being blamed for his failure. Readers today should draw from it the seriousness of speech and the responsibility of those in authority, not a charter for one spouse to overrule the other.

debates.question: When Jesus says 'do not swear at all,' Matthew 5:34, does He forbid all vows and oaths?

views.label: All oaths are forbidden to disciples
views.case: Some Christian traditions, notably the Anabaptists of the Reformation era and later the Quakers, took Jesus' words literally and refused to take any oath, even in court. They point out that James 5:12 repeats the command, 'Above all, my brothers, do not swear,' and that Jesus traces 'anything more' than a plain yes or no to 'the evil one,' Matthew 5:37.

views.label: Evasive and casual oaths are forbidden, not every solemn promise
views.case: Most of the church, including the Reformers, read Jesus as striking at the scribal game of oaths that could be broken on a technicality, Matthew 23:16-22. They note that God Himself swears, Hebrews 6:13-17, that Paul calls God as his witness, Romans 1:9 and 2 Corinthians 1:23, and that Paul kept a vow, Acts 18:18. On this view solemn vows are still lawful when made soberly, but a disciple's ordinary word should be so reliable that oaths add nothing.

debates.bearing: Both views agree that Jesus raises the standard rather than lowering it. Whether or not a believer may ever take an oath, the aim of Numbers 30 and Matthew 5 is the same: that every word spoken before God be true and kept. The debate is about the form of speech, not about whether truthfulness matters.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 2 uses three expressions for a man's commitment. He 'makes a vow,' neder, and 'swears an oath,' shevuah, from shaba, the verb used when God Himself swears to the patriarchs. The third is literally 'to bind a binding upon his soul,' from asar, to tie or bind, the verb used when Joseph had Simeon 'bound before their eyes,' Genesis 42:24. The noun issar, 'pledge' in the BSB, runs through the chapter from verse 2 to verse 14. A vow is pictured as a cord a person ties around his own life.

The command 'he must not break his word' is literally 'he shall not profane his word.' The verb is chalal, to make common or to defile, the same verb used in Leviticus 19:12, 'You must not swear falsely by My name and so profane the name of your God.' A broken vow is not only a failure of honesty; it treats something holy as if it were ordinary.

The positive side is 'he must do everything he has promised,' literally 'according to all that goes out of his mouth.' Verse 12 speaks of 'nothing that came from her lips,' and Deuteronomy 23:23 says, 'follow through on what comes from your lips.' The law's attention is on the mouth as the place where commitments are born.

Verses 6 and 8 add the phrase 'rash promise,' literally 'the rash utterance of her lips,' from bata, to speak thoughtlessly. The verb appears in Leviticus 5:4 for someone who 'swears thoughtlessly with his lips' and in Psalm 106:33, where Moses 'spoke rashly with his lips' at Meribah. Proverbs 12:18 says 'speaking rashly is like a piercing sword.' The law allows for the reality that vows can be made in a rush of feeling.

The verb for the vow standing is qum, to rise or stand, and its causative form means to confirm, verses 13 and 14: the husband who says nothing 'confirms' the vow. It is the same verb in Elkanah's words about Hannah's vowed son, 'may the LORD confirm His word,' 1 Samuel 1:23.

When a vow is lawfully cancelled, 'the LORD will absolve her,' verses 5, 8 and 12. The verb is salach, the ordinary Old Testament word for forgiveness, and in the Old Testament it always has God as its subject. Only God can release a person from a word spoken to Him.

Verse 13 mentions a sworn pledge 'to deny herself,' literally to afflict her soul, with the BSB footnote 'Or to fast.' It is the same expression used for the Day of Atonement in Numbers 29:7. Finally, verse 15 says a husband who cancels late 'will bear her iniquity,' nasa avon, the phrase used of the goat that would 'carry on itself all their iniquities,' Leviticus 16:22, and close to Isaiah 53:12, where the Servant 'bore the sin of many.'

typology.type: The vow that must stand, Numbers 30:2
typology.fulfillment: The man who vows must do 'everything he has promised.' Human vows often fall short, which is why Scripture warns so strongly about rash ones. In Christ the pattern is kept perfectly. All the promises of God 'are Yes in Christ,' 2 Corinthians 1:20, and He Himself became a priest 'with an oath' God will not change, Hebrews 7:20-22. The escalation is that the Son not only keeps His own word but becomes the guarantee of God's. The type falls short because no Israelite could keep every vow perfectly.

typology.type: The one who bears another's iniquity, Numbers 30:15
typology.fulfillment: A husband who nullifies a vow after the time has passed carries the guilt of the broken vow himself, and the woman is spared. Here is a small picture of guilt transferred to the one with authority. It points toward the Servant who 'bore the sin of many,' Isaiah 53:12, and toward Christ, who 'bore our sins in His body on the tree,' 1 Peter 2:24. The contrast is sharp: the husband bears guilt for his own wrong act, while Christ bore guilt He had not incurred.

typology.type: Absolution granted by the LORD, Numbers 30:5, 8, 12
typology.fulfillment: When a vow is lawfully set aside, the text insists that 'the LORD will absolve her.' The release comes from God, not merely from the man. In the gospel, release from debts we cannot pay also comes from God, through Christ, 'in whom we have redemption, the forgiveness of sins,' Colossians 1:14. The escalation is that the law freed from a single rash vow, while Christ frees from the whole weight of guilt, including every broken promise.

typology.type: The psalmist fulfilling his vows in the assembly, Psalm 22:25
typology.fulfillment: The Psalms take up the language of this chapter in public thanksgiving, and Psalm 22 does so after a cry of dereliction that Jesus spoke from the cross. The sufferer who is rescued promises to fulfil his vows before those who fear God. Hebrews 2:12 places words from the same psalm in the mouth of Christ, declaring God's name to His brothers in the assembly. The risen Christ leads His people in the praise the vow looked forward to.

study.christ:
Numbers 30 leads to Christ first through the character of God that it assumes. The law demands that a person 'must not break his word' because God never breaks His. Hebrews 6:17-18 says God confirmed His promise to Abraham with an oath, so that 'by two unchangeable things in which it is impossible for God to lie' His people may be encouraged. Christ is the fulfilment of that sworn faithfulness. Paul tells the Corinthians that the Son of God 'was not Yes and No, but in Him it has always been Yes,' 2 Corinthians 1:19-20, and the risen Lord calls Himself 'the Amen, the faithful and true Witness,' Revelation 3:14.

It leads to Christ through His teaching. The BSB footnote marks Numbers 30:2 as the text behind Matthew 5:33, and Jesus does not dismiss it. He goes deeper. The law regulated special vows; Jesus asks that every word be as reliable as a vow, Matthew 5:37. He also condemned the misuse of vows. In Mark 7:11-13 some declared their goods 'Corban' to escape caring for their parents, and Jesus says they 'nullify the word of God.' Numbers 30 let a father or husband cancel a vow that harmed the household; the scribal tradition let a vow cancel the command to honour father and mother.

It leads to Christ in His own obedience. The Son came to do the Father's will, and He did not revise His costly commitment. In Gethsemane He prayed, 'not as I will, but as You will,' Matthew 26:39. Hebrews 7:20-22 says Jesus became a priest with a divine oath, 'The Lord has sworn and will not change His mind,' and so became 'the guarantee of a better covenant.' His people are secure because both the Father's oath and the Son's obedience stand.

It leads to Christ by the picture of verse 15. The husband who acts too late 'will bear her iniquity.' The phrase recalls the scapegoat and the Servant of Isaiah 53:11-12, who 'will bear their iniquities.' Christ bears iniquity, not because He acted wrongly, but because He took upon Himself what belonged to His bride.

The caution is simple. This chapter is law about vows, not a coded prophecy, and the father and husband are not allegories of Christ. The link lies in the faithfulness of God, which Christ reveals, the teaching of Jesus, which quotes this law, and the language of guilt borne by another, which Scripture itself develops. The one whose every word stands is the one in whom our broken words are forgiven.
study.god:
The chapter reveals a God who listens. The whole law turns on hearing: the father 'hears,' the husband 'hears,' and before either of them the LORD hears every vow made 'to the LORD,' verses 2 and 3. Prayers and promises are not spoken into empty air. Ecclesiastes 5:2 draws the conclusion: 'God is in heaven and you are on earth. So let your words be few.'

He is a God of truth who requires truth. Breaking a vow is to 'profane' one's word, verse 2, the same verb used for profaning God's name in Leviticus 19:12. Human speech before Him borrows something of His holiness. That is why He can 'surely require it,' Deuteronomy 23:21. His own word is the pattern: He swears by Himself because there is no one greater, Hebrews 6:13, and He cannot lie, Hebrews 6:18.

He is also a God of order in households. He does not ignore the realities of family responsibility; He regulates them. The one day limit of verses 5, 7, 12 and 14 prevents both hasty control and endless uncertainty. The rule of verse 15, that a husband who acts late bears her guilt, shows that God holds those with authority more accountable, not less.

He is a God who forgives. The verb for 'absolve' is the Old Testament's word for divine forgiveness, reserved for God alone. When a woman's vow is lawfully cancelled, He does not leave her with a vague sense of failure; He releases her. This is the same God who, in Numbers 14:20, answered Moses' plea for the people with 'I have pardoned them as you requested.'

The law holds together justice and mercy. Vows are binding, yet there is provision for release. Words matter, yet God knows that people speak rashly. He neither shrugs at broken promises nor crushes the weak under them.

For worship, the chapter calls believers to praise God for keeping every word He has spoken, to be careful and sincere in what they promise Him in song, prayer and vow, and to bring their failures to Him rather than hiding them. The God who hears every vow is also the God who can absolve.

crossReferences.note: Moses sets the balance that frames Numbers 30. Vowing is voluntary, and refraining is no sin, but a vow made must be kept without delay, for the LORD 'will surely require it of you.' The phrase 'what comes from your lips' echoes Numbers 30:12, locating the commitment in the mouth.

The Teacher applies the law of vows to the heart. Be slow to speak before God, keep your vow, and do not tell the messenger it was a mistake. The warning shows the danger Numbers 30 guards against: promises made hastily and then explained away at the sanctuary.

Jephthah's rash vow is a tragic case of the danger Numbers 30 recognises. He promises a burnt offering of whatever comes out of his house and then cries, 'I have given my word to the LORD and cannot take it back.' The story warns against vowing without thought, the 'rash promise' of Numbers 30:6.

Hannah vows to give her son to the LORD, and Elkanah, her husband, lets the vow stand, saying 'may the LORD confirm His word.' Read against Numbers 30:10-14, his words are the confirmation the law describes, and Hannah's faithfulness gives Israel Samuel.

The one who may dwell on God's holy hill 'does not revise a costly oath.' This is the heart of Numbers 30:2 turned into a portrait of godly character: a person whose word holds even when keeping it hurts. Integrity of speech is part of fitness for God's presence.

An earlier law treats the person who 'swears thoughtlessly with his lips' as guilty once he realises it, and requires confession and a sin offering. It uses the same verb as the 'rash promise' of Numbers 30:6 and 8, showing that rash speech before God is not trivial but needs atonement.

Jesus summarises Numbers 30:2 and Deuteronomy 23:21-23, 'Do not break your oath, but fulfill your vows to the Lord,' and then deepens it: disciples should need no oath, because their plain yes and no are true. He moves the focus from special vows to all speech.

Jesus exposes the misuse of vows. By declaring something 'Corban,' devoted to God, a son could refuse to support his parents. Jesus says this nullifies God's word. Numbers 30 allowed a vow to be cancelled to protect a household; the tradition let a vow override the command to honour parents.

God swore by Himself to Abraham to make the unchanging nature of His purpose clear. The seriousness of human vows in Numbers 30 reflects the seriousness of God's own word. Because it is impossible for God to lie, those who have fled to Him have strong encouragement.

Paul defends his own reliability by pointing to Christ, who 'was not Yes and No,' for 'all the promises of God are Yes in Christ.' The ideal of Numbers 30:2, a word that never breaks, is perfectly realised in the Son of God, and through Him believers say their Amen.

study.oneStory:
Words have been at the centre of the story from the beginning. God spoke creation into being, Genesis 1:3, and humanity fell when a word from God was doubted and twisted, Genesis 3:1-4. Ever since, people have made promises and broken them. Numbers 30 sits in that long story as a law that takes human words seriously because God's own words are always true.

The chapter answers something in the wilderness narrative. Israel had promised at Sinai, 'We will do everything that the LORD has spoken,' Exodus 19:8, and then broken that promise again and again. A new generation on the edge of the land is taught that a word spoken to God binds, and that God Himself holds the speaker to it.

The story that follows shows how hard that is. Jephthah keeps a terrible vow, Saul makes a foolish oath, Israel swears loyalty to the covenant and then forgets it, and by Jesus' day vows have become a way of dodging duty. The problem is not the law but the human heart, which cannot keep its word perfectly.

The answer comes in Christ, the faithful Witness, in whom every promise of God is Yes, 2 Corinthians 1:20. He keeps His Father's will at the cost of the cross, and He bears the iniquity of those whose words have failed. Through Him believers are forgiven for broken promises and given the Spirit so that their yes can become yes.

The story ends in a new creation where speech is finally true. Of the redeemed it is said, 'no lie was found in their mouths,' Revelation 14:5, and liars have no place in the city, Revelation 21:27. The One seated on the throne declares that His words 'are faithful and true,' Revelation 21:5. The vows of Numbers 30 looked for a people whose word could be trusted. In the new creation that people stands before the God whose word has never failed.

quiz.q: According to verse 2, what is required of a man who makes a vow to the LORD?

options.text: He must not break his word; he must do everything he has promised.
options.note: Verse 2 states this requirement directly and without qualification.

options.text: He may reconsider the vow at any time without consequence.
options.note: The text states the opposite, that his word must not be broken.

options.text: He must have the vow approved by the priest before it is binding.
options.note: No such priestly approval process is mentioned for a man's own vow.

options.text: No specific requirement is given.
options.note: Verse 2 gives a clear and direct requirement.

quiz.q: What happens to a young woman's vow if her father hears of it and says nothing, according to verse 4?

options.text: All her vows and pledges shall stand.
options.note: Verse 4 states this exactly.

options.text: The vow is automatically canceled.
options.note: The opposite is true; silence confirms the vow rather than canceling it.

options.text: The vow must be renewed publicly each year.
options.note: No such renewal requirement is mentioned in this law.

options.text: No outcome is specified.
options.note: Verse 4 clearly specifies the outcome.

quiz.q: Within what timeframe could a father or husband nullify a dependent woman's vow, according to this chapter?

options.text: Only on the day he first heard of it.
options.note: This time limit is repeated in verses 5, 7, 8, and 12.

options.text: At any point during her lifetime.
options.note: The law restricts this power specifically to the day he first hears of the vow.

options.text: Only within one year of the vow being made.
options.note: The text specifies the single day he hears of it, not a full year.

options.text: No time limit is given.
options.note: The single-day limit is stated repeatedly throughout the chapter.

quiz.q: According to verse 9, whose vow was always fully binding regardless of any household authority?

options.text: The vow of a widow or divorced woman.
options.note: Verse 9 states this explicitly.

options.text: The vow of a young daughter still in her father's house.
options.note: Her vow could be nullified by her father within the specified timeframe, unlike the vow described in verse 9.

options.text: The vow of a married woman still under her husband's authority.
options.note: Her vow could similarly be nullified by her husband within the specified timeframe.

options.text: No exception to household authority is mentioned.
options.note: Verse 9 states this exception directly.

quiz.q: According to verse 15, what happens if a husband nullifies his wife's vow well after the day he first heard of it?

options.text: He himself bears the guilt of her broken vow.
options.note: Verse 15 states this consequence directly.

options.text: The vow is nullified with no further consequence to anyone.
options.note: The text specifies that delayed nullification transfers the guilt to the husband himself.

options.text: The wife alone bears full responsibility regardless of timing.
options.note: The text specifically shifts responsibility to the husband in this case of delayed nullification.

options.text: No consequence is mentioned for late nullification.
options.note: Verse 15 addresses this consequence explicitly.

questions: This law treats every vow spoken to God with total seriousness. Where in your own life do you speak commitments to God more casually than you should?
A father or husband's silence itself functioned as confirmation of a vow. Where might your own silence be quietly confirming a commitment you have not fully thought through?
Jesus later taught that simple, truthful speech should make elaborate vows unnecessary. How consistent is your everyday yes and no with what you actually follow through on?
This law provided real protection for those under another's household authority. Where do you need to extend care and protection to someone more vulnerable than yourself?
Christ is called the Amen, the one whose word never fails. Where do you need to rest more fully in the certainty that His promises to you will be kept completely?

translationNotes.note: Vow and oath, though closely related, are technically distinct in Hebrew law, a neder typically dedicating something to God while a shevuah, oath, is a sworn pledge; this chapter treats both with the same binding seriousness.

The LORD will absolve her, in cases of a nullified vow, shows that even a rightly canceled vow required God's own release, underscoring that a vow's binding power flowed from its being made to Him, not merely from household regulation.

The closing summary explicitly limits the law's scope to relationships between a husband and wife and between a father and an unmarried daughter still in his household, showing the text itself frames this as household-specific case law rather than a universal statute governing all vows.
